fullText:
Summary: Alumex PLC (ALUM.N0000), Sri Lanka's largest aluminium extrusion maker and a Hayleys company, is earning well again: profit for the six months to September 2026 nearly quadrupled. But at Rs 16.40 the share trades at 1.8x its NAV of Rs 8.98, and its trailing P/E of 9.3x rests on one exceptional quarter (January–March 2026, EPS Rs 1.40). Alumex's profits swing widely with aluminium prices and demand (a loss in 2022/23, almost nothing in 2023/24), and its borrowings are nearly twice its equity. On normal earnings the methods put fair value at about Rs 8.40, so the price is about 95% above it. I'd buy at up to about Rs 7.20 and treat under Rs 6.30 as a strong buy.

Price and key figures
Price: Rs 16.40 (CSE closing price, 2026-11-06). Please check it live. In July–September 2026 it traded between Rs 15.70 and Rs 17.90. In the year to March 2026 it ranged from Rs 13.50 (April 2025) to Rs 22.70 (October 2025) and closed at Rs 16.60.
Six months to 30 September 2026 (unaudited): revenue rose 13% to Rs 8.60bn and profit rose to Rs 268mn from Rs 69mn. EPS was Rs 0.45 against Rs 0.12. The September quarter earned Rs 118mn (EPS Rs 0.20), on a gross margin of 21%.
Year to March 2026 (audited): revenue Rs 16.94bn (up 18%), profit Rs 863mn (flat), EPS Rs 1.44 (Rs 1.45), ROE 17%, dividends Rs 0.47. Almost all of that year's profit came in January–March 2026 (EPS Rs 1.40), when aluminium prices jumped. It also included Rs 229mn of insurance income from the 2024/25 fire at the Ekala plant.
Debt: borrowings Rs 10.1bn and net debt about Rs 9.6bn at September 2026, about 1.8x equity. Short-term loans rose by Rs 2.4bn in the half as inventory grew by Rs 2.8bn. Interest cover was only 2.2x last year.
Cycle: EPS over ten years was Rs 1.26, 0.61, 0.21, 0.05, 1.40, 1.92, -0.02, 0.31, 1.45 and 1.44 (2016/17 to 2025/26), an average of about Rs 0.86. ROE averaged about 16.5%.

Methods
NAV (Rs 8.98): 1.8x.
Return on equity: 17% in 2025/26 and 21% in 2024/25 (the latter helped by fire insurance), but 5% in 2023/24 and below zero in 2022/23.
P/E: 9.3x trailing EPS of Rs 1.77, including the exceptional March 2026 quarter. Year-end P/E: 11.5x (2026), 10.5x (2025).
Dividends: Rs 0.47 for 2025/26, a 2.9% yield, a third of profit; Rs 0.20 has been paid for this year.
Justified price to book: Rs 4.0 / 7.3 / 12.7, weighted Rs 7.4.
P/E method: Rs 6.0 / 10.8 / 17.1, weighted Rs 10.6.
Residual income: Rs 3.5 / 6.9 / 14.3, weighted Rs 7.4.

Alumex pays out a third of its profit, so a dividend model understates it, and its cash flow swings with aluminium stock levels, so a cash-flow DCF isn't reliable. Price to book and residual income are stricter because the base-case ROE (15%) is below the cost of equity (17%).

Assumptions (bear / base / bull)
Cost of equity: 18.5% / 17% / 15.5% (a cyclical, highly geared manufacturer).
Long-run ROE (price to book and residual income): 11% / 15% / 19%.
Long-term growth: 5% / 6% / 7%.
EPS for the year to March 2027 × P/E: 0.85 × 7 / 1.20 × 9 / 1.55 × 11.
Average of the three methods: Rs 4.5 / Rs 8.3 / Rs 14.7.
Common: Sri Lankan 7–10-year government bonds yield about 12% (October 2026). The base case assumes the second half earns about Rs 0.75 a share, well below last year's exceptional Rs 1.32. Payout 33%.

Fair value and buy price
Fair value: weighting 30/50/20 gives about Rs 8.40 (0.9x NAV), so Rs 16.40 is about 95% above it.
Buy price: a 15% margin of safety gives Rs 7.20, and 25% gives Rs 6.30.
Plan for 500 shares: 200 at up to Rs 8.40, 150 at up to Rs 7.20 and 150 at up to Rs 6.30. That averages about Rs 7.41, about Rs 3,705, against Rs 8,200 at Rs 16.40.
Realism: Rs 8.40 needs about a 49% fall. The share was Rs 9.50 in April 2024 and Rs 7.20 in March 2020, so it has been there in bad years, but it isn't likely soon unless earnings fall back.

Sensitivity (residual income base case, Rs per share)
Cost of equity 15.5%: 4.4 / 8.4 / 14.0 for long-run ROE of 11% / 15% / 19%.
Cost of equity 17%: 3.7 / 6.9 / 11.4.
Cost of equity 18.5%: 3.2 / 5.8 / 9.5.
Today's price needs ROE of well over 20% for many years.

What would change my view
Supports a higher value: profits staying near the March 2026 quarter's level; borrowings falling as stock is sold; exports to Europe and Australia growing further; a building boom in Sri Lanka.
Supports a lower value: aluminium prices falling (stock bought at high prices loses value); construction slowing; interest rates rising on its large short-term loans; more of the cyclical losses seen in 2019–2020 and 2022–2024; competition from Swisstek and imports.

These are my estimates from the annual reports for the years to March 2025 and March 2026 and the interim reports to September 2026. The September 2026 interim report is a scanned image, so I read its figures by text recognition; check any figure that matters. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.
